title: GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)
licence: EU law. Titles are the official article headings; purpose, guidance, audit questions and typical evidence are our own words. Read the official text on EUR-Lex.

requirements.title: Chapter II · Principles
requirements.purpose: Sets the ground rules every use of personal data must meet: fairness, a valid reason, and extra care for sensitive data.

requirements.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data
requirements.purpose: Sets the core rules for all personal data use: lawful, fair and open handling, fixed purposes, only the data needed, accuracy, limited retention and security, with the controller able to prove it follows them.
requirements.guidance: Turn each principle into a working habit. State a purpose before collecting any data, drop fields nobody uses, and set retention periods per data category with a named owner. Review them at intervals you set; many organisations review yearly. Auditors commonly find forms that ask for more than needed, retention schedules that exist on paper but are never run, and no evidence that anyone checks accuracy. Keep a short principles checklist inside your project and supplier onboarding steps so it is applied before data starts flowing.
questions: How do you decide which personal data a new process may collect, and for what purpose?
How do you check that data collected for one purpose is not reused for an unrelated one?
Where are retention periods defined and who deletes data when they expire?
How do you keep personal data accurate over time?
What records would you show us to prove these principles are applied?
evidence: Data protection policy approved by management
Retention schedule with owners and review dates
Records of deletion or anonymisation runs
Data minimisation review of forms and systems
Training records for staff handling personal data

requirements.title: Lawfulness of processing
requirements.purpose: Requires every use of personal data to rest on at least one of the six legal bases, chosen and recorded before processing starts, so you can explain why you are allowed to do it.
requirements.guidance: Map each processing purpose to the basis that genuinely fits: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests, and write the reasoning down. Where you rely on legitimate interests, keep a short balancing test showing whose interests were weighed; public authorities cannot use it for their official tasks. Do not default to consent, since it can be withdrawn and is rarely free in an employment relationship. Before reusing data for a new purpose, check whether the new purpose is compatible with the original. Auditors often find bases never chosen deliberately or swapped after the fact. Reflect the chosen basis in your privacy notices and your record of processing.
questions: What legal basis applies to each of your main processing activities?
Where you rely on legitimate interests, where is the balancing test?
How do you handle a change of purpose for existing data?
Does your privacy notice match the bases you actually use?
evidence: Register of processing with a legal basis per activity
Approved procedure for choosing a legal basis

requirements.title: Conditions for consent
requirements.purpose: Makes sure that where you rely on consent, it is freely given, specific and can be proven and withdrawn as easily as it was given.
requirements.guidance: Use clear, separate opt-in wording with no pre-ticked boxes and no bundling with unrelated terms. Store who consented, when, to what text and through which channel. Provide a simple withdrawal route, such as a link or setting, and act on it promptly. Typical findings are consent logs without the wording shown at the time, consent tied to using a service, and withdrawal that needs an email to a mailbox nobody reads. Re-check consent when purposes change.
questions: How do you record that a person consented and to which wording?
How can someone withdraw consent, and how quickly is it applied?
Is consent ever a condition of receiving a service it is not needed for?
How do you keep consent records for older sign-ups?
evidence: Consent log with timestamp, version of text and channel
Screenshots or copies of consent forms by version
Withdrawal procedure and sample completed withdrawals

requirements.title: Processing of special categories of personal data
requirements.purpose: Prohibits using sensitive data such as health, religious or political beliefs, sexual orientation, union membership or biometrics used for identification unless a specific exception applies, because misuse causes greater harm.
requirements.guidance: First identify whether you hold any sensitive data at all, including indirectly such as sickness absence reasons or dietary needs that reveal health. For each case record the exception relied on in addition to the ordinary legal basis under Article 6. Several exceptions, for example employment and social security, only work if national law provides for them, and national law may add conditions for health, genetic and biometric data, so check your local rules. Restrict access tightly and consider stronger security and shorter retention. Auditors often find sensitive data in free-text fields, shared drives or HR spreadsheets that nobody classified. Include these cases in your impact assessment screening.
questions: Which sensitive categories of data do you process, and where are they stored?
Which exception do you rely on for each, and what Article 6 basis sits alongside it?
Where an exception depends on national law, which provision do you rely on?
Who has access to this data and why?
How do you stop sensitive details appearing in free-text notes?
evidence: Access control lists for sensitive data stores
Staff guidance on handling sensitive data

requirements.title: Chapter III · Rights of the data subject
requirements.purpose: Gives people control over their data and obliges you to be open about what you do with it and to respond to their requests.

requirements.title: Transparent information and modalities for data subject rights
requirements.purpose: Requires you to communicate in plain language and to handle requests from individuals promptly, free of charge in most cases and after checking identity.
requirements.guidance: Set up one route for rights requests, such as a web form and mailbox, and log every request with received date, due date and outcome. Agree who triages, who gathers data and who signs off. Where you have reasonable doubts about identity, ask for proportionate proof, not a stack of documents. Reply within one month; you may extend by up to two further months for complex or numerous requests, but must tell the person within the first month and say why. If you refuse, explain why and mention the right to complain to the authority. Charging or refusing is only possible for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, and you must be able to show that. Auditors find missing logs, late replies and requests lost in general inboxes.
questions: How does someone submit a rights request and who receives it?
How do you track deadlines and extensions?
How do you verify the requester without collecting too much?
What happens when a request is refused, and what is the person told?
evidence: Request log with dates and outcomes
Training records for those handling requests

requirements.title: Information where data are collected from the data subject
requirements.purpose: Ensures people are told who you are, why you use their data, how long you keep it and what rights they have at the moment you collect it.
requirements.guidance: Provide a layered privacy notice at each collection point, such as sign-up forms, job applications and cameras. Cover who you are and how to reach you and any DPO, purposes with legal bases and the legitimate interests pursued, recipients, international transfers, retention, rights including withdrawal of consent and complaint, whether providing the data is required and what happens if not, and any automated decision-making. Keep it in plain language and keep versions. Pitfalls include notices copied from other organisations, missing retention information, and staff or candidate data with no notice at all. Before reusing data for a new purpose, tell people first.
questions: Where do people see your notice when you collect their data?
Does the notice list purposes, legal bases, retention and recipients accurately?
Is there a separate notice for employees and job applicants?
How do you update the notice when processing changes?
evidence: Current privacy notices with version history
Screenshots of notices at collection points
Change log linking process changes to notice updates
Review sign-off by the privacy owner

requirements.title: Information where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject
requirements.purpose: Ensures people are informed when you receive their data from someone else, such as a partner, a broker or a public source.
requirements.guidance: Identify flows where data arrives from third parties, such as purchased leads, referrals, customer-supplied contacts or public registers. Tell the individuals within a reasonable time and at the latest within one month, or earlier if you first contact them or pass the data on. Include the categories of data and where they came from. Exceptions are narrow: the person already has the information, informing is impossible or would take disproportionate effort, the collection is set by law, or professional secrecy applies. Record the reasoning, and where effort is disproportionate still protect people, for example by publishing the information. Auditors often find notices only for direct collection and nothing for indirect sources.
questions: Which processes receive personal data from third parties?
How and when are those individuals informed, and how is the one-month limit tracked?
Where you rely on an exception, where is the reasoning recorded?
Do you tell people the source and categories of their data?
evidence: Records of notices sent with dates
Supplier and partner contracts covering notification duties

requirements.title: Right of access by the data subject
requirements.purpose: Lets people ask for confirmation of whether you hold their data, a copy of it and details about how it is used.
requirements.guidance: Know where personal data lives, including email, backups, chat tools and paper files, so a search can be completed within the deadline. Prepare a standard response pack listing purposes, recipients, retention and rights, plus the copy itself. Check whether the data contains information about other people and redact where needed. Pitfalls are incomplete searches, missing systems and sending data without confirming identity. Keep a record of what was supplied.
questions: How do you search all systems for one person's data?
How do you protect other people's information in the response?
What is included in your response beyond a copy of the data?
How long does a typical request take you?
evidence: Data location map used for searches
Completed request files with redaction notes
Request log showing times to respond

requirements.title: Right to rectification
requirements.purpose: Lets people have inaccurate or incomplete data corrected without delay.
requirements.guidance: Provide an easy route for corrections, ideally a self-service account page plus a contact for other cases. Update every system holding the data, not just the first one you notice, and tell the person when done. Where you cannot confirm the new details, note that clearly. Auditors find corrections made in the main system but not in exports, spreadsheets or marketing tools. Link this process to the process for notifying recipients.
questions: How can people ask you to correct their data?
How do you ensure the correction reaches all systems?
How do you handle disputed accuracy?
Who do you tell about the correction?
evidence: Log of correction requests and outcomes
System list showing where corrections are propagated

requirements.title: Right to erasure
requirements.purpose: Lets people have their data deleted in defined situations, for example when it is no longer needed or consent is withdrawn.
requirements.guidance: Define when erasure applies and when you must keep data, such as for tax or legal claims, and record the reason for any refusal. Build deletion into systems so that it covers databases, backups on their normal cycle, logs and processors. Where data was made public, take reasonable steps to inform others using it. Typical gaps are copies in spreadsheets, supplier systems and backups with no documented expiry. Test deletion end to end occasionally.
questions: How do you decide whether an erasure request must be granted?
Which systems and suppliers hold copies, and how are they cleared?
How are backups dealt with?
What do you tell the person if you must keep some data?
evidence: Test results of deletion in key systems

requirements.title: Right to restriction of processing
requirements.purpose: Lets people pause certain uses of their data, for example while accuracy or an objection is being checked.
requirements.guidance: Decide how a restriction is technically applied, such as a flag that blocks use except for storage, and who can set and lift it. Make sure restricted records are excluded from mailings, reports and automated decisions. Tell the person before lifting a restriction. This right is rarely used, so organisations often have no mechanism at all, which an auditor will notice. A simple flag and a one-page procedure is usually enough for a small company.
questions: How would you mark a record as restricted?
How do you stop restricted data being used in other processes?
Who may lift a restriction and what notice is given?
Has the process been tested?
evidence: Screenshot or description of the restriction flag
Test record of a restricted item

requirements.title: Notification regarding rectification, erasure or restriction
requirements.purpose: Requires you to pass on corrections, deletions and restrictions to those you disclosed the data to, and to tell the person who they are if asked.
requirements.guidance: Keep a record of recipients for each data set so you can find who needs to be told. Add a notification step to the correction, erasure and restriction procedures, with a contact at each recipient. Where notifying is impossible or disproportionate, record why. Common failings are no recipient list and processors never informed. Contracts with suppliers should oblige them to act on such notices.
questions: How do you know who received a person's data?
Who sends notifications to recipients and when?
How do you handle recipients who do not respond?
Can you tell a person who the recipients were if they ask?
evidence: Notification emails or tickets sent to recipients

requirements.title: Right to data portability
requirements.purpose: Lets people receive data they gave you in a usable format and have it sent to another provider where feasible.
requirements.guidance: Check whether it applies: it covers data the person provided, including activity data you observed, where processing is based on consent or contract and is automated. It does not cover data you derived or inferred, or processing for a public task. Prepare an export in a structured, machine-readable format such as CSV or JSON and test it. Offer direct transfer to another provider where technically feasible. Where the export contains information about other people, such as contacts or shared messages, consider whether handing it over would harm them. Document why a request was out of scope when you refuse.
questions: Which of your processes fall within portability?
In what format do you provide the data?
Can you send it directly to another provider if asked?
How do you decide whether data about other people can be included in the export?

requirements.title: Right to object
requirements.purpose: Lets people object to uses based on legitimate interests or public tasks, and to stop direct marketing at any time.
requirements.guidance: Make the objection route visible in notices and marketing messages, with a one-click unsubscribe. For other objections, assess whether you have compelling grounds that override and record the decision. Apply marketing suppressions across every tool and keep a suppression list that survives list imports. Auditors often find unsubscribes that do not reach all systems and re-imports that reverse them.
questions: How do people object, and where is that explained?
How do you evaluate objections to legitimate interests processing?
How are marketing opt-outs enforced across systems?
How do you prevent re-importing suppressed contacts?
evidence: Marketing email footers and unsubscribe test

requirements.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
requirements.purpose: Stops significant decisions about people being made solely by automated means, unless a narrow ground applies and safeguards such as human review and a right to contest are in place.
requirements.guidance: List any automated decisions that materially affect people, for example credit checks, recruitment screening or account blocking. For each, check whether a person is genuinely involved or merely rubber-stamps. Where the rule applies, rely on an allowed ground, give meaningful information about the logic and offer a route to human review and to challenge. Auditors find scoring tools adopted without anyone asking whether this applies. Record the assessment.
questions: Which decisions about people are made automatically?
Is a human involved in a meaningful way?
How do you explain the logic to affected people?
How can someone contest an automated decision?
evidence: Privacy notice text on logic and consequences

requirements.title: Chapter IV · Controller and processor
requirements.purpose: Covers the organisational duties of anyone handling personal data: accountability, design, contracts, records, security, breaches and oversight roles.

requirements.title: Responsibility of the controller
requirements.purpose: Makes the organisation responsible for putting in place measures that ensure and can show that its processing complies.
requirements.guidance: Accountability means being able to prove compliance, not merely claim it. Keep a lightweight privacy programme: policies, a named owner, a risk-based plan, training and regular reviews with management. Scale measures to the risk of the data you handle. Auditors typically find policies with no owner, no review cycle and no evidence they are followed. Report privacy metrics, such as open requests and incidents, to management at set intervals.
questions: Who is accountable for data protection in your organisation?
How do you show management reviews the programme?
How do you decide that measures are appropriate to risk?
How do you check that policies are followed?
evidence: Data protection policy and programme plan
Role description for the privacy owner

requirements.title: Data protection by design and by default
requirements.purpose: Requires privacy to be built into products and processes from the start, with the most protective settings as the default.
requirements.guidance: Add a privacy step to project and change management: ask what data is needed, who sees it, how long it is kept and whether settings default to the least data. Use techniques such as pseudonymisation, access limits and short retention. Keep a short design record per project. Auditors find privacy considered only after launch, or default settings that share data widely. A simple checklist at design review catches most of this.
questions: How is privacy considered when new systems or features are designed?
What are the default settings for new users?
Which technical measures limit data exposure?
Where are design decisions recorded?
evidence: Change management tickets with privacy sign-off

requirements.title: Processor
requirements.purpose: Requires you to use only processors who give sufficient guarantees and to bind them with a written contract.
requirements.guidance: Keep a list of every supplier that handles personal data on your behalf and check each has a signed data processing agreement covering the subject, duration and nature of the processing, documented instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processors, assistance, return or deletion and audits. Do due diligence before onboarding and revisit periodically. If you act as a processor for your customers, the same article sets your own duties, such as getting approval for sub-processors and flagging instructions you believe are unlawful. Common findings are missing agreements with smaller tools, unapproved sub-processors and no exit plan for data. Align this with supplier management.
questions: How do you identify and list processors?
Does every processor have a compliant contract?
How do you assess a supplier's security before use?
How do you control sub-processors and data return at exit?

requirements.title: Records of processing activities
requirements.purpose: Requires a written record of what personal data you process and why, so you and regulators can see the whole picture.
requirements.guidance: Maintain a register listing for each activity the purpose, categories of people and data, recipients, transfers and their safeguards, retention and a description of security measures, plus your contact and DPO details. If you also act as a processor, keep a separate record of processing you carry out for clients. Assign an owner per activity and review on a set cycle and on any change. Organisations with fewer than 250 staff are only exempt if processing is occasional, unlikely to create risk and excludes special-category and criminal offence data; regular HR or customer processing is not occasional, so most must keep a record. Auditors find registers that are out of date, stop at the IT view or lack retention and transfer details. The authority can ask to see it.
questions: Who maintains the record and how often is it reviewed?
Does it cover every department, including HR and marketing?
Does it list retention periods and international transfers?
If you act as a processor, where is your processor record?
How do changes in business processes reach the record?
evidence: Record of processing activities with version
Link between register and privacy notices
Change management evidence updating the register

requirements.title: Security of processing
requirements.purpose: Requires technical and organisational security that fits the risk, covering confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience.
requirements.guidance: Base measures on a documented risk assessment and cover access control, encryption where sensible, backups, patching, logging, staff awareness and supplier security. Test that controls work, for example restore tests and phishing exercises. Keep it proportionate to the data and the harm if lost. Auditors often find shared accounts, untested backups and no evidence of reviews. If you already run an information security management system, map it here.
questions: How did you decide which security measures are appropriate?
How do you ensure only authorised people access personal data?
How often do you test backups and recovery?
How do you review security after changes or incidents?
evidence: Penetration test or vulnerability scan reports

requirements.title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
requirements.purpose: Requires you to report a personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people.
requirements.guidance: Have an incident procedure that lets anyone report a suspected breach quickly, with a named person to assess risk and decide on notification. The default is to notify; only a breach unlikely to create risk may stay internal. The clock starts when you become aware, so detection and escalation speed matter. If facts are incomplete, notify with what you know and add the rest in phases; if you miss 72 hours, explain the delay. Log every breach, including those not reported, with the reasoning. Processors must tell you without undue delay, so check contracts. If you are also in scope of NIS2, the same event may need a separate 24-hour early warning.
questions: How do staff report a suspected breach and to whom?
Who decides whether the authority must be told?
How do you meet the 72-hour window out of hours?
Where do you record breaches that were not reported?
evidence: Breach drill or tabletop exercise records

requirements.title: Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject
requirements.purpose: Requires you to tell affected people promptly when a breach is likely to put them at high risk, so they can protect themselves.
requirements.guidance: Add a high-risk decision step to the breach procedure with criteria such as sensitivity, volume and ease of misuse. Prepare plain-language notice templates saying what happened, likely effects, what you are doing, what people can do and a contact point. Choose a channel that actually reaches them. You need not tell people if the data was unintelligible to others, for example properly encrypted, or if you have since removed the high risk; where contacting each person would take disproportionate effort, make a public announcement instead. Record that reasoning, because the authority can still order you to inform people. Auditors find undocumented decisions and vague notices.
questions: How do you decide whether a breach is high risk to individuals?
How quickly can you contact all affected people?
What advice do you give them?
Where is the decision documented?

requirements.title: Data protection impact assessment
requirements.purpose: Requires a structured risk assessment before starting processing likely to be high risk, such as large-scale profiling or sensitive data.
requirements.guidance: Create a short screening questionnaire used at project start and a template for full assessments covering the description, necessity and proportionality, risks to people and mitigations. Check your supervisory authority's published list of processing that always needs an assessment; as a rule of thumb, two or more high-risk factors such as profiling, sensitive data, monitoring or new technology usually mean one is required. Seek the DPO's advice where you have one and, where relevant, the views of affected groups. If high risk remains after mitigation, consult the authority before starting. Auditors find assessments done after launch or screening that never triggers. Revisit assessments when processing changes.
questions: How do you decide whether an assessment is required, and which authority list do you use?
Who completes and approves them, and how is the DPO involved?
How are residual high risks handled?
How do you revisit assessments after changes?

requirements.title: Designation of the data protection officer
requirements.purpose: Requires a DPO for public bodies and for organisations whose core activities involve large-scale regular and systematic monitoring of people or large-scale processing of special-category or criminal offence data.
requirements.guidance: Document your assessment of whether appointment is mandatory, including what your core activities are and whether processing is large scale, and keep it even when the answer is no. National law can widen the duty; for example German law requires a DPO in many smaller organisations, so check local rules. If you appoint voluntarily, the same rules on position and tasks apply. The DPO needs expert knowledge, can be an employee or an external provider, and one DPO may serve a group if easily reachable from each entity. Publish their contact details and notify them to the authority. Auditors find reasoning missing and contact details not registered.
questions: Have you assessed whether you must appoint a DPO, under the GDPR and national law?
Where is the decision and its reasoning recorded?
Are the DPO's contact details published and notified to the authority?
What qualifications and data protection expertise does the DPO have?

requirements.title: Position of the data protection officer
requirements.purpose: Makes sure the DPO is involved in relevant matters, has resources and independence, and reports to top management.
requirements.guidance: Give the DPO access to management, time, budget and information. They should not be told how to reach conclusions or be penalised for advice. Avoid conflicts of interest, for example a head of IT or marketing acting as DPO. Provide a route for individuals to contact them. Auditors find DPOs consulted late or without enough hours. Document how and when the DPO is brought into projects and incidents.
questions: How is the DPO involved in new projects and incidents?
What resources and time are allocated?
Who does the DPO report to?
How do you avoid conflicts of interest?
evidence: DPO job description with reporting line
Records of DPO advice and responses

requirements.title: Tasks of the data protection officer
requirements.purpose: Defines the DPO's work: advising, monitoring compliance, supporting assessments and acting as contact for the authority.
requirements.guidance: Agree a work plan for a period you set, often a year, covering training, monitoring checks, advice on assessments and liaison with the regulator. Keep records of advice given and follow-up. Report to management at intervals you set; many DPOs report at least yearly. Auditors find DPO roles that exist only on paper, with no monitoring activity or reports. Remember the DPO advises and monitors; the organisation stays responsible for compliance.
questions: What does the DPO's work plan include, and what period does it cover?
How does the DPO monitor compliance?
How is advice recorded and followed up?
How does the DPO report to management?
evidence: DPO work plan for the period you set

requirements.title: Chapter V · Transfers of personal data to third countries
requirements.purpose: Controls sending personal data outside the EEA so that people's protection travels with their data.

requirements.title: General principle for transfers
requirements.purpose: Sets the rule that data may leave the EEA only if the chapter's conditions are met, so protection is not lost along the way.
requirements.guidance: Identify every flow outside the EEA, including cloud hosting, support access, group companies and software that phones home. For each, record the destination and the mechanism you rely on. Include onward transfers by suppliers. Auditors often find unnoticed transfers through SaaS tools and remote support staff. Keep the transfer map linked to the processing register and revisit when suppliers change.
questions: Which suppliers and systems send data outside the EEA?
What mechanism covers each transfer?
How do you find out about changes in supplier locations?
How do you cover remote access from other countries?

requirements.title: Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision
requirements.purpose: Allows data to flow to countries or frameworks the European Commission has found to offer adequate protection.
requirements.guidance: Check the current list of adequacy decisions before relying on one, and note any conditions; for example, transfers to the United States rely on adequacy only where the recipient is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Record the date checked and monitor for changes, reviews or court challenges. Keep a fallback mechanism in mind. Auditors find reliance on a decision that does not cover the recipient or that has since changed. Note the basis in your register and contracts.
questions: Which transfers rely on adequacy?
How do you confirm that the recipient is covered?
How do you monitor for changes to adequacy decisions?
What is your fallback if the decision lapses?
evidence: Record of adequacy checks with dates

requirements.title: Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards
requirements.purpose: Allows transfers without adequacy if safeguards such as standard contractual clauses give people enforceable protection.
requirements.guidance: Sign the correct standard clauses module for the parties' roles and complete the annexes with real details. Carry out and keep a transfer risk assessment covering the destination's laws and your supplemental measures such as encryption. Review when circumstances change. Auditors find unsigned or incomplete clauses and no assessment. Make sure sub-processor transfers are also covered.
questions: Which transfers use standard clauses or other safeguards?
Are the annexes completed accurately?
Where is the transfer risk assessment?
What supplementary measures do you apply?

requirements.title: Binding corporate rules
requirements.purpose: Allows transfers within a corporate group under internal rules approved by the regulator.
requirements.guidance: Most small and mid-sized companies will not use this route because approval takes considerable time. If your group has approved rules, verify that they cover the entities and processing in question and that staff are trained on them. Keep a copy of the approval and track changes. If you do not use them, record that and rely on another mechanism.
questions: Does your group have approved binding corporate rules?
Do they cover the transfers you make?
How are staff trained on them?
How do you handle changes to group membership?

requirements.title: Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law
requirements.purpose: States that a foreign court or authority order does not by itself justify sending data abroad unless an international agreement supports it.
requirements.guidance: Create a short procedure for handling requests from non-EU authorities: who receives them, who involves legal advice and how the decision is recorded. Do not hand over data on the basis of the request alone. Challenge or narrow requests where appropriate. Auditors find no procedure and staff unsure what to do. Make sure processors must notify you of such requests.
questions: Who handles requests from foreign courts or authorities?
How do you check the legal basis before disclosing?
How do processors tell you about such requests?
Have you received any, and how were they handled?

requirements.title: Derogations for specific situations
requirements.purpose: Provides narrow exceptions, such as explicit consent or contract necessity, for transfers where no other mechanism exists.
requirements.guidance: Treat these as a last resort for occasional transfers, not a routine route. Record which exception applies and why the stronger mechanisms were not available. For consent, it must be explicit and given after people are told of the risks. The final fallback, compelling legitimate interests, is only for rare, non-repetitive transfers about a limited number of people, and you must inform the supervisory authority and the people concerned. Auditors challenge organisations that use exceptions for regular large-scale transfers. Review any reliance periodically and move to standard clauses where possible.
questions: Do you rely on any exceptions, and for which transfers?
Why could another mechanism not be used?
How do you inform people about the risks where consent is used?
If you rely on compelling legitimate interests, how were the authority and the people informed?
How often do you review this reliance?
evidence: Notice to the supervisory authority for compelling legitimate interests transfers
Plan to move to a stronger mechanism
